title: John's head (Mark 6:14–29)
hook: a drunken promise at a party and the death of the Baptist, told in flashback

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve sent out in pairs. Your line was less in the bag, more trust. Today makes twenty-six weeks.

While the twelve are out in the villages, the news reaches the palace. Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, hears what's being done in Jesus's name. People are guessing who Jesus is: Elijah come back, one of the old prophets. Herod has his own answer, and it's a guilty one. It's John, he says, the one I beheaded. He's risen. Then Mark stops the story and flashes back, to tell how John the Baptist died.
screen: `NEWS REACHES THE PALACE.` → `IT'S JOHN, RISEN.` → `A FLASHBACK.`

segments.voice: Herod had married Herodias, who had been married to his brother. John told him to his face that it wasn't lawful, so Herod had him chained in prison. But here's Mark's twist: Herod was fascinated by John. He feared him, knew he was a good and holy man, and listened to him gladly, even though it left him troubled. Then comes Herod's birthday: a banquet for the officials, the officers, the leading men of Galilee. The daughter of Herodias dances, and it pleases everyone. And Herod, in front of all his guests, swears an open-ended promise, in the old King James Bible: "Whatsoever thou shalt ask of me, I will give it thee, unto the half of my kingdom." The girl goes out to her mother. What should I ask? The answer: the head of John the Baptist. On a platter, she adds. "And the king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath's sake, and for their sakes which sat with him, he would not reject her." He does it anyway, because backing down in front of the room would cost him face. It's done. John's disciples come for the body and bury him. In the King James text, Mark never names the girl. The name Salome comes from the historian Josephus, who lists Herodias's daughter but doesn't tell this story. Mark doesn't say Herod was drunk either, only that it was a feast. But the scene has the feel of it: a big promise, made to impress, and one man too proud to take it back. That closes a week: Legion. Go home and tell. The hem of his garment. Talitha koum. The carpenter. Travel light. And John's head.
screen: `JOHN IN CHAINS, HEROD LISTENING.` · `ASK ME FOR ANYTHING.` · `EXCEEDING SORRY, YET FOR HIS OATH.` · `THE NAME SALOME IS FROM JOSEPHUS.`

segments.voice: Think of promises you've made lately, I'll call you back, I'll fix it this weekend, and notice any made to look good or to end a conversation. Choose one that matters to someone, one you've let slide, and picture keeping it; if you pray, ask for help to keep your word. If a promise was careless, it's all right to admit it and make a better one.
John's head. The price of a ruler's reckless oath at a feast, told by Mark as a flashback.
Your line: careless words cost lives. A promise made to impress can cost more than it's worth. Half a year of days, and here you are.

howItsDone: Christians honor John the Baptist as a prophet who died for speaking the truth; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches remember his beheading with a feast on August 29.

chat.says: Why did Herod have John the Baptist killed if he respected him?
options: He'd sworn a big promise before his guests and was too proud to take it back.
Herod was drunk and didn't understand what he'd agreed to give.
John had escaped from prison, and Herod's guards caught him at the feast.
chat.meaning: Herod feared John and knew he was holy, yet kept a reckless oath at a feast to save face before the room.

Herod Antipas.meaning: the ruler of Galilee who had John beheaded

Herodias.meaning: Herod's wife, once married to his brother

Salome.meaning: the name Josephus gives Herodias's daughter; Mark doesn't name her

Josephus.meaning: a historian who lists Herodias's daughter by name

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut 'only flashback' / 'nowhere else' (hook, word, trapdoor), the invented 'goes pale' and 'you can hear it'; 'Mark never names the girl' narrowed to the King James text, since some Greek manuscripts of 6:22 call her Herodias; Josephus named as naming the daughter, not telling the dance. The outline says 'a drunken promise'; Mark doesn't say Herod was drunk, and the script says so plainly ('only that it was a feast').
'Mark's only flashback' is a common claim; confirm it holds (6:17–29 is the standard example).
Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.4) names Salome as Herodias's daughter; 18.5.2 places John's death at Machaerus. Confirm references.
Mark calls Herod 'king'; he was tetrarch. Script calls him 'the ruler of Galilee'.
Feast of the Beheading of John the Baptist, August 29 (Catholic, Anglican; Orthodox same date on their calendar). Confirm.
